content:
If your one-year FD at SBI, HDFC, or ICICI is due for renewal this month, you're getting 6.25 percent. That's a full percentage point below where rates were a year ago. Short-duration debt funds are now returning 7 to 7.6 percent, taxed the same way as an FD. So this isn't a hypothetical question. It's what you have to decide when the banker slides the renewal form across.

  • Major bank one-year FD rates are at 6.25 percent as of October 2026, down sharply from 2024 and 2025
  • Liquid funds return 6.5 to 7 percent; short-duration debt funds land around 7 to 7.6 percent
  • The debt fund tax advantage was removed in April 2023: both FDs and debt funds are now taxed at your slab rate
  • FDs remain the better choice when safety and simplicity matter more than an extra half-percent return
  • Small finance bank FDs pay up to 8.5 percent for two-to-three year tenures, often the best deal for amounts under Rs 5 lakh

Why your FD rate just dropped by a full percent

The RBI cut its repo rate four times between February 2025 and June 2026, taking it from 6.5 percent to 5.25 percent. Each cut nudged banks to lower what they pay depositors. Big banks moved first and fastest. The one-year rate at SBI is now 6.25 percent, the lowest it's been since late 2021.

The rate compression occured faster than most FD investors expected. In early 2024, locking in a 7.5 percent two-year FD felt smart. Renewing it now at 6.25 percent means roughly Rs 6,250 less per year on every lakh you have parked. Multiply that across a few lakhs and it adds up.

The banks that haven't followed as aggressively are the small finance banks. Unity, Suryoday, and Shivalik are still offering 8.1 to 8.5 percent on two-year-plus tenures. More on those below.

Is the tax advantage for debt funds still real in 2026?

No. Since April 2023, gains from debt funds are taxed at your income tax slab rate, exactly like FD interest. The old long-term capital gains benefit at 20 percent with indexation was removed. So if you're still reading articles that call debt funds more tax-efficient, they're referencing rules that no longer exist.

This is the single biggest thing to get straight before you decide. Before April 2023, debt fund investors could qualify for LTCG with indexation, a real advantage for anyone in the 30 percent bracket. Those older units may still carry some of that treatment. New money you put in today doesn't. The gains you recieve from a fresh debt fund investment are taxed at your slab rate, same as FD interest.

The returns advantage has grown enough that debt funds are still worth considering. Just not for tax reasons.

When it actually makes sense to stay in the FD

If you need the money in less than three months, an FD is simpler and not much worse. If you depend on regular interest payouts, FDs handle that cleanly. And if your total at any one bank is under Rs 5 lakh, the DICGC guarantee means your principal is completely safe regardless of what the bank does.

Retirees living partly off FD interest are a good example. The quarterly payout option is a clean, predictable income stream. Moving to a mutual fund, even a liquid fund, means withdrawing units manually, which is a seperate step not everyone wants to manage.

One more case worth knowing: amounts above Rs 5 lakh at a single bank. DICGC only insures up to that limit. If you have Rs 20 lakh in one bank's FD, only Rs 5 lakh is protected. Spreading across banks addresses this, and so does moving part of the amount to a debt fund.

Frequently Asked Questions

Should I break my existing FD early to move to a debt fund?

Probably not unless maturity is far out and the break penalty is small. Breaking an FD typically costs 0.5 to 1 percent of the interest, which can erase most of the return advantage from switching. Wait for maturity, then redirect the money.

Are liquid funds actually safe?

Liquid funds invest mostly in government securities and top-rated commercial paper with very short maturities. They're not insured the way FDs are, but credit risk is very low. The category has been stable since the 2019 cleanup of poorly managed debt funds.

What exactly is a short-duration fund?

It's a debt mutual fund holding bonds that mature in one to three years. More sensitive to interest rate changes than a liquid fund, but for most market conditions the returns smooth out over a one-to-two year holding period. Returns run slightly higher than liquid funds.

Do small finance bank FDs make sense in 2026?

For amounts under Rs 5 lakh, yes. Unity, Suryoday, and Shivalik are offering 8.1 to 8.5 percent on two-to-three year tenures, which beats most alternatives. Keeping each deposit within the Rs 5 lakh DICGC limit is the standard way to manage the added risk.

Will debt fund returns keep falling if the RBI cuts rates again?

Liquid fund returns track the overnight rate closely, so yes, more cuts mean lower yields. Short-duration funds are less sensitive. Most analysts expect one or two more cuts in this cycle, which could push liquid fund returns down another 25 to 50 basis points over 12 months.

The short version

Renewing at 6.25 percent when short-duration funds are returning 7 to 7.6 percent is leaving real money behind. The tax argument that once favored debt funds is gone since 2023. What remains is a straightforward return advantage and better liquidity. FDs still make sense if you need a guarantee, rely on payouts, or can't be bothered managing a fund account. And for amounts under Rs 5 lakh where a small finance bank is accessible, that 8 to 8.5 percent rate is often the best option few people are actually using.
